source_text: Sed remisso Alexandro cum suis syllogismis, quos in argumentationibus torquet, etiam cum psalmis Valentini, quos magna impudentia quasi idonei alicuius auctoris interserit, ad unam iam lineam congressionem dirigamus, an carnem Christus ex virgine acceperit, ut hoc praecipue modo humanam eam constet, si ex humana matrice substantiam traxit. Quamquam liquuit iam et de nomine hominis et de statu qualitatis et de sensu tractationis et de exitu passionis humanam constitisse. Ante omnia autem commendanda erit ratio quae praefuit ut dei filius de virgine nasceretur. Nove nasci debebat novae nativitatis dedicator, de qua signum daturus dominus ab Esaia praedicabatur. Quod est istud signum? Ecce virgo concipiet in utero, et pariet filium. Concepit igitur virgo et peperit Emmanuelem, nobiscum deum. Haec est nativitas nova, dum homo nascitur in deo. In quo homine deus natus est carne antiqui seminis suscepta sine semine antiquo, ut illam novo semine, id est spiritaliter, reformaret exclusis antiquitatis sordibus expiatam. Sed tota novitas ista, sicut et iu omnibus, de veteri figurata est, rationali per virginem dispositione homine domino nascente. Virgo erat "adhuc terra nondum opere compressa, nondum sementi subacta; ex ea hominem factum accipimus a deo in an imam vivam. Igitur si primus Adam ita traditur, merito sequens, vel novissimus Adam, ut apostolus dixit, proinde de terra, id est carne nondum generationi resignata, in spiritum vivificantem a deo est prolatus. Et tamen Ð¿Ðµ mihi vacet incursus nominis Adae, unde Christus Adam ab apostolo dictus est, si terreni non fuit census homo eius? Sed et hic ratio defendit. quod deus imaginem et similitudinem suam a diabolo captam aemula operatione recuperavit. In virginem enim adhuc Evam irrepserat verbum aedificatorium mortis. In virginem aeque introducendum erat dei verbum exstructorium vitae, ut quod per eiusmodi sexum abierat in perditionem per eundem sexum redigeretur in salutem. Credideral Eva serpenti: credidit Maria Gahrieli. Quod illa credendo deliquit, hace credendo delevit. Sed Eva nihil tunc concepit in utero ex diaboli verbo. Immo concepit. Nam exinde ut abiecta pareret et in doloribus pareret verbum diaboli semen illi fuit. Enixa est denique diabolum fratricidam. Contra Maria eum edidit qui carnalem fratrem Israel interemptorem suum salvum quandoque praestaret. In vulvam ergo deus verbum suum detulit, bonum fratrem, ut memoriam mali fratris eraderet. Inde prodeundum fuit Christo ad salutem hominis quo homo iam damnatus intraverat.
thought_title: The New Birth from the Virgin, Prefigured in Adam and Eve
orientation: Tertullian has set aside Alexander and Valentinus and now argues directly that Christ took flesh from the Virgin, showing that this new birth was fitting and was prefigured in the creation of Adam and the fall of Eve.
pass_a_gloss: But with Alexander dismissed, with his syllogisms, which he twists in his argumentations, and also with the psalms of Valentinus, which he inserts with great impudence as if they were of some suitable author, let us now direct the engagement to one line, whether Christ received flesh from the virgin, so that it may be established as human in this especially way, if he drew substance from a human womb. Although it has already become clear both from the name of man and from the state of his quality and from the sense of his treatment and from the outcome of his passion that it was established as human. But before all things the reason will have to be commended which was in charge, that the Son of God should be born from a virgin. He had to be born in a new way, the inaugurator of a new birth, about which the Lord, about to give a sign, was proclaimed by Isaiah. What is this sign? Behold, a virgin will conceive in the womb, and will bear a son. Therefore the virgin conceived and bore Immanuel, God with us. This is the new birth, while man is born in God. In this man God was born, flesh of the ancient seed having been taken up without the ancient seed, so that he might reform it with a new seed, that is spiritually, after it had been cleansed, the filth of antiquity having been excluded. But all this newness, just as also in all things, was prefigured from the old, by a rational arrangement through a virgin, the Lord being born as man. The virgin earth was still not yet pressed by work, not yet subdued for sowing; from it we receive that man was made by God into a living soul. Therefore if the first Adam is so handed down, deservedly the second, or the last Adam, as the apostle said, was in like manner brought forth from the earth, that is from flesh not yet opened for generation, into a life-giving spirit by God. And yet let not the incursion of the name of Adam be empty for me, whence Christ was called Adam by the apostle, if his man was not of earthly origin? But here too reason defends it, that God recovered his image and likeness, captured by the devil, by a rival operation. For into the virgin Eve had crept the word that builds death. Into a virgin equally had to be introduced the Word of God that builds life, so that what had gone away into perdition through this kind of sex might be brought back into salvation through the same sex. Eve had believed the serpent: Mary believed Gabriel. What that one by believing did wrong, this one by believing wiped out. But Eve then conceived nothing in the womb from the word of the devil. No, she conceived. For from then on, so that she might bear as an outcast and bear in pains, the word of the devil was seed to her. She brought forth at last the devil, the fratricide. In contrast Mary brought forth him who would at some time make safe his carnal brother Israel, his own killer. Therefore God brought his Word into the womb, a good brother, so that he might erase the memory of the evil brother. From there Christ had to come forth for the salvation of man, where man already condemned had entered.

pass_b_english: But let me dismiss Alexander with his syllogisms, which he twists in his arguments, and also the psalms of Valentinus, which he inserts with great impudence as if they came from some worthy author. Let me direct our engagement to a single line: did Christ receive flesh from the virgin, so that it is established as human in this particular way, if he drew its substance from a human womb? Although it has already become clear from the name of man, from the condition of its qualities, from the sense of its treatment, and from the outcome of its passion that it was human. Before everything, however, I must commend the reason that presided over the Son of God's birth from a virgin. He had to be born in a new way, the inaugurator of a new birth, about which the Lord was proclaimed by Isaiah as the one who would give a sign. What is that sign? "Behold, a virgin will conceive in the womb and bear a son" (Isaiah 7:14). Therefore the virgin conceived and bore Immanuel, God with us. This is the new birth, while man is born in God. In this man God was born, flesh of the ancient seed having been taken up without the ancient seed, so that he might reform it with new seed, that is, spiritually, cleansed with the filth of antiquity excluded. But all this newness, as in everything, was prefigured from the old, by a rational arrangement through a virgin, when the Lord was born as man. The earth was still a virgin, "not yet pressed by work, not yet subdued for sowing; from it we receive man made by God into a living soul" (Genesis 2:7). Therefore if the first Adam is so handed down, rightly the following, or last Adam, as the apostle said, was brought forth by God from the earth, that is, flesh not yet opened for generation, into a life-giving spirit (1 Corinthians 15:45). And yet let me not leave unexamined the intrusion of the name Adam — why Christ was called Adam by the apostle, if his man was not of earthly origin? But here too reason defends it: that God recovered his image and likeness, captured by the devil, by a rival operation. For into the virgin Eve the word that builds death had crept in. Into a virgin equally the Word that builds life had to be introduced, so that what had gone into perdition through this kind of sex might be brought back into salvation through the same sex. Eve had believed the serpent: Mary believed Gabriel. What the former did wrong by believing, the latter wiped out by believing. But Eve then conceived nothing in her womb from the devil's word. No, she conceived. For from then on, so that she might bear as an outcast and bear in pains, the devil's word was seed to her. She brought forth at last a fratricidal devil. Against this, Mary brought forth him who would one day make safe his carnal brother Israel, his own killer. Therefore God brought his Word into the womb, a good brother, to erase the memory of the evil brother. Christ had to come forth for the salvation of man from the place where man, already condemned, had entered.

problems.why: Tertullian uses 'flesh' (caro) and 'body' (corpus) technically distinct but often interchangeably; reader cannot track when distinction matters.
problems.fix: Note when 'body' means soma/corpus vs. when 'flesh' means sarx/caro.

problems.why: Satan's word to Eve; 'builds' is odd for 'brings about/causes.'
Cain called 'fratricide devil'; awkward construction, possibly 'devilish fratricide' or 'fratricidal devil.'

problems.quote: not yet pressed by work, not yet subdued for sowing
problems.why: Genesis 2:5 paraphrase; not exact quotation. 'Pressed by work' is not standard.
Marcion is called 'that man from Pontus' without explicit identification; a first-time reader may not know this is Marcion.
problems.fix: Add '(Marcion)' after 'that man from Pontus' on first use.

fixed: The glossary problem about 'flesh' vs 'body' is not a translation error in this section; the English uses 'flesh' consistently for caro, and no 'body' term appears here, so no edit is needed.
The source 'verbum aedificatorium mortis' uses 'aedificatorium' (building), but 'builds death' is awkward in English; 'brings death' better conveys the sense of causing death while remaining natural.
The source 'diabolum fratricidam' means 'the fratricidal devil' (Cain as the devil's offspring); 'a fratricide devil' is awkward, so 'a fratricidal devil' is clearer.
The Genesis 2:5 paraphrase is not an exact quotation; the English already presents it as a quotation with a citation, but the source is a paraphrase, so no edit is needed to the wording itself.
The 'that man from Pontus' problem does not appear in this section; no edit is needed.

problems.quote: from which Christ was called Adam by the apostle, if his man was not of earthly origin?
problems.source_quote: unde Christus Adam ab apostolo dictus est, si terreni non fuit census homo eius
problems.why: unde introduces why Christ is called Adam, not a relative 'from which'.
problems.fix: why Christ was called Adam by the apostle, if his man was not of earthly origin.
problems.ruling: "unde Christus Adam ab apostolo dictus est" is causal 'whence/why'; 'from which Christ was called Adam' misreads as relative and muddles the sentence's logic.

problems.ruling: 'aedificatorium mortis' means 'building/constructing death', set against 'exstructorium vitae'. 'Brings death' loses the building parallel and the contrast with the Word that builds life.

last_rejected.quote: The earth was still a virgin
last_rejected.why: The Latin says the virgin (Mary) is described with earth imagery; the English shifts the subject to the earth itself, altering who is the virgin.
last_rejected.fix: Render as "The virgin was still like untouched earth" or similar, preserving the virgin as the subject.

last_rejected.quote: "not yet pressed by work, not yet subdued for sowing; from it we receive man made by God into a living soul" (Genesis 2:7)
last_rejected.source_quote: Virgo erat adhuc terra nondum opere compressa, nondum sementi subacta; ex ea hominem factum accipimus a deo in animam vivam.
last_rejected.why: The uncultivated virgin earth and "we receive" are Tertullian's words. Genesis 2:7 only says man became a living soul.
last_rejected.fix: The earth was still a virgin, not yet pressed by work or subdued for sowing; from it, we hold, God made man a living soul (Genesis 2:7).
last_rejected.ruling: Tertullian's own text quotes/paraphrases Gen 2:7 ('in animam vivam'); the English cites it as Genesis 2:7 with quotes, a conventional attribution of the allusion, not a mistranslation of the Latin.
